test.title: An address is not a place

texts.title: An address is not a place

paragraphs.text: A postal code looks like a description of a place and is nothing of the kind. It is an instruction to a sorting machine, invented because the machine cannot read a street name reliably and can read a short string of characters at speed. Everything that codes are now used for — finding an insurance quote, drawing a school catchment, describing a neighbourhood in a newspaper — is a second life the system was never designed for, and most of the arguments about codes come from that mismatch.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first systems were wartime expedients. Several countries divided their largest cities into numbered districts in the 1930s and 1940s so that inexperienced staff could sort mail that experienced staff had previously sorted from memory. The numbers were coarse, they applied only in cities, and they were not intended to survive; the reason they did is that postal volumes went on rising and the supply of people willing to memorise street lists did not.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: National codes came with machines. A sorting machine of the 1960s could read printed digits, so a code that covered the whole country and identified a delivery office was worth the cost of teaching the public to use it. Advertising campaigns of remarkable persistence followed, with songs, mascots and letters returned to senders who had left the code out. Within a decade the habit was established in most of the countries that tried it, which is a reminder that a national habit can be created if there is a machine behind it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Designs diverge sharply in how much geography they encode. A purely numeric code that runs from one end of a country to the other, with the first digit a region and the last a delivery route, is easy to remember and tells a stranger roughly where you live. An alphanumeric code can be much finer, identifying a side of a street or a single large building, and is correspondingly harder to remember. The fine systems save the post office more money and give away more information about the household, and both of those consequences were understood at the time.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The second life began when other industries discovered that a code is a cheap way to aggregate people. Insurers price by code, retailers site shops by code, and marketing databases describe codes in terms of the households they contain. The description is statistical and is applied to individuals, which is where it goes wrong: a person in a poor code is quoted a price that reflects the code rather than the person, and a person who moves a hundred metres may find their premium changes for no reason connected to them.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Codes also freeze in a way that places do not. A boundary drawn for the convenience of a delivery round in 1968 still separates two halves of a street, and the data attached to it accumulates: a hospital catchment, a bus route, a statistical series that would be broken if the boundary moved. Post offices are reluctant to change codes for exactly this reason, and the result is a geography of the country that is slightly wrong everywhere and is used as though it were exact.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Not everywhere has addresses at all. In many fast-growing cities, whole districts have no street names and no numbers, which makes deliveries, ambulances and voter registration equally difficult. The responses have been inventive: schemes that give every few metres of the world a short name derived from its coordinates, community projects that number houses and paint the numbers, and postal services that deliver to a described location rather than an address. Each works, and each depends on someone maintaining it, which is the part that usually fails.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The lesson is about what happens to an administrative convenience when it is used as a fact. A code was a way of moving letters; it became a proxy for wealth, for risk and for identity, and in several countries it is now a protected characteristic in some kinds of decision precisely because it stood in for characteristics that were already protected. Systems built for one purpose are borrowed for others, and the borrowing is rarely examined until somebody is refused something because of a string of characters printed on an envelope.
paragraphs.label: H

topic.en: What the text is about: where postal codes came from, how other industries borrowed them and what happens when an administrative convenience becomes a fact.

topic.ru: О чём текст: откуда взялись почтовые коды, как их позаимствовали другие отрасли и что бывает, когда служебная условность становится фактом.
